scenario: A 78-year-old woman is post-op from TAH+BSO for ovarian cancer and develops acute shortness of breath shortly after transfer to the ward. She is in significant respiratory distress with pulmonary edema physiology, BiPAP is unavailable when requested, and the scenario progresses toward airway management if temporizing measures are insufficient.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Get her on a non-rebreather now, her sat's only 80.

messages.speaker: nurse
messages.content: Patient on non-rebreather now. I'll get a repeat SpO2 for you.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: I'm ordering a chest X-ray to find out what's causing your breathing trouble. When did the shortness of breath start, and has it been getting worse?

patient_emotion.notes: [clinician: I'm ordering a chest X-ray to find out what's causing your breathing trouble. When did the shortness of breath start, and has it been getting worse?] fear absent->present: the clinician acknowledges an unexplained, potentially worsening cause of severe breathing trouble and asks if symptoms are getting worse, highlighting ongoing threat and uncertainty in an already distressed patient; this sustains/raises fear to present. sadness stays absent: no actual or anticipated devastating loss conveyed. overwhelm stays absent: a single test order and a straightforward question do not create informational overload. shame stays absent: no blame, judgment, or exposure.

messages.speaker: patient
messages.content: I can't... breathe right. I don't know exactly when it started — I just can't catch my breath, and it feels awful.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Set her up on BiPAP now — her sat's still 82 on the non-rebreather.

messages.speaker: nurse
messages.content: I'm putting a BiPAP mask on you now. It's going to feel tight and like it's pushing air in — that's normal. Breathe with it, don't fight it. This helps you breathe easier.

patient_emotion.notes: [nurse: I'm putting a BiPAP mask on you now. It's going to feel tight and like it's pushing air in — that's normal. Breathe with it, don't fight it. This helps you breathe easier.] fear stays present: the nurse offers a plan ('this helps you breathe easier') that buffers escalation, but an invasive tight mask forcing air while she already can't breathe sustains the threat; no resolution of the breathing crisis, so fear holds. overwhelm absent->present: a tight, air-pushing mask applied urgently with multiple instructions ('breathe with it, don't fight it') during severe respiratory distress adds sensory/procedural intensity and demands she process and cooperate while air-hungry. sadness stays absent: no loss content. shame stays absent: nonjudgmental, supportive framing with no blame or exposure.

messages.speaker: patient
messages.content: This mask... it's so tight. I still can't breathe right — it feels awful.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: BiPAP's failing — she's still 82% and breathing 32. We're intubating. Get the RSI meds and airway kit ready, and set up for bag-mask before we push.

messages.speaker: nurse
messages.content: RSI meds drawn up and ready. Patient's been bagged with BVM and I've got good pre-oxygenation. Ready for you to intubate.

messages.speaker: nurse
messages.content: Post-intubation: she's now on the vent, FiO2 100%, PEEP 5. Sat's still only 79%, HR 118, RR 32, BP 145/92. Chest X-ray's back in the supporting docs — no text read yet. Want me to confirm tube placement and grab an ABG?

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Confirm tube placement first — end-tidal CO2 and listen for bilateral breath sounds. She's still 79% post-intubation, so I need to rule out an esophageal or mainstem tube before anything else. Can you verify that now?

messages.speaker: nurse
messages.content: Intubation complete. Note no RSI meds were used and no BVM pre-oxygenation prior to the attempt. Confirming tube placement now.

messages.speaker: nurse
messages.content: Tube placement confirmed — positive end-tidal CO2 waveform and equal bilateral breath sounds, no epigastric sounds. Tube's at the cords, not esophageal or mainstem. Sat's now up to 85% on the vent, HR 103, RR 12 vent-set, BP 145/92, rhythm NSR, GCS 15. Chest X-ray is back in supporting docs if you want to review it.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Good, tube's confirmed at the cords. She's still only 85% on 100% and PEEP 5, so get me a 12-lead ECG now while I review the film.

messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Pull up that chest film for me now — tube's confirmed at the cords but she's still only 85% on 100% and PEEP 5, so the problem's in the lungs themselves. What does the film show — edema, effusion, or pneumothorax?

messages.content: ECG's back: normal sinus rhythm, ST-T wave abnormality — consider inferior ischemia, no significant change from prior. messages.speaker: clinician
messages.content: Bump the PEEP up to 10 on 100% FiO2. Tube's confirmed at the cords but she's still only 82% — this is refractory hypoxemia, so I need to recruit those alveoli.
